sections.title: How does the Pivot point calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pivot point calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports high price in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the method); then you type in the open price, the Resistance level 3 (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (R3) (R3) (R3) (R3) (R3) (Result), the Support level 3 (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (Result) and the Support level 3 (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (Result).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pivot point calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

High price=-close price − low price + 3 × pivot point (PP)
Resistance level 1 (r 1)=-low price + 2 × pivot point (PP)
Resistance level 2 (r 2)=pivot point (PP) + Resistance level 1 (r 1) (r 1) (r 1) (r 1) (r 1) (r 1) (R1) (R1) (R1) (R1) (R1) − Support level 1 (s 1) (s 1) (s 1) (s 1) (s 1) (s 1) (S1) (S1) (S1) (S1) (S1)

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Method set to Floor, Low price = 10, Close price = 10 and Pivot point (PP) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives High price = 10, Resistance level 4 (r 4) = 10, Resistance level 3 (r 3) = 10 and Resistance level 2 (r 2) = 10.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: High price = 10, Resistance level 4 (r 4) = 10, Resistance level 3 (r 3) = 10 and Resistance level 2 (r 2) = 10 should be roughly the size you expected from Method set to Floor and Low price = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pivot point calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the open price, the Resistance level 3 (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (r 3) (R3) (R3) (R3) (R3) (R3) and the Support level 3 (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (s 3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) (S3) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Pivot point calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns high price, derived from the open price, the resistance level 3 (R3) and the support level 3 (S3). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pivot point calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the open price, the resistance level 3 (R3) and the support level 3 (S3), which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter open price in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Open price opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports High price = 10. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pivot point calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
